subject: physics

items.q: An electron moves horizontally into the region between two horizontal parallel plates, midway between them and at right angles to the uniform electric field between the plates. It is deflected towards the positive plate. Gravity is negligible. Which describes the motion of the electron while it is between the plates?
items.correct: A parabola: its horizontal velocity is constant as it accelerates towards the positive plate
items.misconception: A circular arc at constant speed, with the force at right angles to its velocity
items.why: The circular path of a charge in a magnetic field is the iconic image of a particle 'bent by a field', and electric and magnetic deflection are taught side by side, so students transfer the circle and the constant speed to the electric case. A circle needs a force that is always perpendicular to the velocity and so keeps changing direction; that is the magnetic force. The electric force in a uniform field has a fixed direction, like gravity near the Earth's surface, so the path is a parabola and the speed increases.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field
items.random_wrong: A straight line at an angle, moving towards the positive plate at a steady velocity

items.q: Two horizontal parallel plates, 2.5 cm apart in a vacuum, have a potential difference of 150 V between them. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of an electron between the plates? Gravity is negligible. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
items.correct: 1.1 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻²
items.misconception: 1.1 × 10¹³ m s⁻²
items.why:
A systematic procedural error reported in examiners' reports: students copy numbers straight from the question, especially when the unit prefix is small print or the numbers look convenient. Convert first: 2.5 cm = 0.025 m, 40 mT = 0.040 T. An unconverted value changes the answer by a power of ten (a factor of 100 for cm, 1000 for mT), which an order-of-magnitude check will usually expose.

Working: E = V/d = 150 V / 0.025 m = 6.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹. F = eE and a = F/m_e = eE/m_e = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(6.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹) / (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) = 1.05 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻² ≈ 1.1 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻².
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field

items.q: Two parallel plates, 2.0 cm apart in a vacuum, have a potential difference of 500 V between them. An electron is released from rest at the negative plate and accelerates across the gap. What is its speed when it reaches the positive plate? Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
items.why:
A procedural error common in multi-step calculations: the factor ½ is lost when the energy equation is rearranged, especially when it is combined with another equation such as r = mv/(qB). Kinetic energy is ½mv², so qV = ½mv² and v = √(2qV/m). Dropping the ½ makes v too small by a factor of √2. In the charge-to-mass determination, where qV = ½mv² is combined with r = mv/(qB), it gives q/m = V/(B²r²), half the true value 2V/(B²r²).

Working: Work done by the field = eV = ΔE_k. eV = ½m_ev² ⇒ v = √(2eV/m_e) = √(2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 500 V / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) = √(1.76 × 10¹⁴ m² s⁻²) = 1.33 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (Equivalently E = V/d = 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, a = eE/m_e, v² = 2ad: the separation cancels.)
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field
items.working: Work done by the field = eV = ΔE_k. eV = ½m_ev² ⇒ v = √(2eV/m_e) = √(2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 500 V / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) = √(1.76 × 10¹⁴ m² s⁻²) = 1.33 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (Equivalently E = V/d = 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, a = eE/m_e, v² = 2ad: the separation cancels.)

items.q: A proton moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field that is perpendicular to its velocity. No other forces act on it. Which statement about the kinetic energy of the proton is correct?
items.correct: It stays constant, because the magnetic force is perpendicular to its velocity.
items.misconception: It varies continuously around the circle, as the direction of the proton's velocity keeps changing.
items.why: E_k = ½mv² is written with the symbol for velocity, and students who have learned that velocity is a vector assume that anything calculated from it changes whenever the velocity changes. Kinetic energy is a scalar that depends on v², the square of the speed. A particle moving in a circle at constant speed has a continuously changing velocity but a constant kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.random_wrong: It increases steadily, because the magnetic force accelerates the proton and so does work on it.

items.q: Positive ions of a single type, initially at rest, are accelerated through a potential difference of 1500 V. They then enter a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.25 T at right angles to their velocity, travel through a semicircle and strike a detector 6.3 cm from the point where they entered the field. What is the charge-to-mass ratio q/m of the ions?
items.correct: 4.8 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹
items.misconception: 1.2 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹
items.why:
A procedural slip in mass-spectrometer and e/m problems: students substitute the only length given without picturing the semicircle; the same error occurs when a diameter is used for a radius in circular-motion and wire problems. Sketch the semicircle: it starts and ends at opposite ends of a diameter. Halve the measured distance to obtain r before substituting into r = mv/(qB) or q/m = 2V/(B²r²).

Working: Semicircle ⇒ 6.3 cm is the diameter, so r = 3.15 cm = 0.0315 m. Acceleration: qV = ½mv² ⇒ v² = 2qV/m. In the field: qvB = mv²/r ⇒ r = mv/(qB) ⇒ r² = m²v²/(q²B²) = 2mV/(qB²). Hence q/m = 2V/(B²r²) = (2 × 1500 V)/((0.25 T)² × (0.0315 m)²) = 3000/(0.0625 × 9.92 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.8 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.working: Semicircle ⇒ 6.3 cm is the diameter, so r = 3.15 cm = 0.0315 m. Acceleration: qV = ½mv² ⇒ v² = 2qV/m. In the field: qvB = mv²/r ⇒ r = mv/(qB) ⇒ r² = m²v²/(q²B²) = 2mV/(qB²). Hence q/m = 2V/(B²r²) = (2 × 1500 V)/((0.25 T)² × (0.0315 m)²) = 3000/(0.0625 × 9.92 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.8 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹.

items.q: A proton moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field that is perpendicular to its velocity. A second proton moves at twice the speed of the first, perpendicular to the same field. Compared with the first proton, what are the radius of the second proton's circle and the time it takes to complete one revolution?
items.correct: Radius doubled; time for one revolution unchanged
items.misconception: Radius halved; time for one revolution reduced to a quarter
items.why: Students reason from one relation only (F = qvB increases with v) and link 'more force' with 'more turning', without considering that the force needed to turn a faster particle also increases. Compare the force available with the force needed: qvB = mv²/r. Doubling v doubles qvB but quadruples mv² for the same radius, so the radius must double. Faster particles move in larger circles.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.random_wrong: Radius unchanged; time for one revolution halved

items.q: Protons pass undeflected through a velocity selector in which two parallel plates 1.5 cm apart have a potential difference of 600 V between them and a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.050 T acts at right angles both to the electric field and to the velocity of the protons. The protons then enter a region containing only a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.050 T, at right angles to their velocity, travel through a semicircle and strike a detector. How far is the detector from the point where the protons entered this region? Gravity is negligible. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m_p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
items.why:
In everyday language 'voltage' means how strong an electrical supply is, and conceptual surveys of electricity and magnetism show students routinely confuse potential with field. The symbols V and E also both appear in 'V m⁻¹'. Potential difference is energy per unit charge (J C⁻¹ = V); field strength is force per unit charge (N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹). For parallel plates E = V/d, so the same potential difference produces a stronger field when the plates are closer together.

Working: Selector: E = V/d = 600 V / 0.015 m = 4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Undeflected ⇒ resultant force zero ⇒ eE = evB ⇒ v = E/B = (4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹)/(0.050 T) = 8.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Second region: evB = m_pv²/r ⇒ r = m_pv/(eB) = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(8.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹)/((1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(0.050 T)) = 0.167 m. After a semicircle the detector is one diameter from the entry point: 2r = 0.334 m ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹ m.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields
items.working: Selector: E = V/d = 600 V / 0.015 m = 4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Undeflected ⇒ resultant force zero ⇒ eE = evB ⇒ v = E/B = (4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹)/(0.050 T) = 8.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Second region: evB = m_pv²/r ⇒ r = m_pv/(eB) = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(8.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹)/((1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(0.050 T)) = 0.167 m. After a semicircle the detector is one diameter from the entry point: 2r = 0.334 m ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹ m.

items.q: In a velocity selector, uniform electric and magnetic fields act at right angles to each other and to the velocity of the particles, so that the electric and magnetic forces on a proton are in opposite directions. Protons moving at speed v₀ pass straight through undeflected. Gravity is negligible. Which statement about this velocity selector is correct?
items.correct: A proton faster than v₀ is deflected in the direction of the magnetic force on it.
items.misconception: A proton of any speed passes undeflected, as neither of the forces depends on its speed.
items.why: Electric and magnetic forces are taught together and the electric force qE really is independent of speed; students carry the same expectation over to the magnetic force. The magnetic force acts only on moving charges and is proportional to their speed: F = qvB sin θ. In crossed fields the electric force qE is fixed but the magnetic force qvB grows with v, so the forces balance only at one speed, v = E/B.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields
items.random_wrong: Only particles with a proton's charge-to-mass ratio can pass undeflected at speed v₀.

items.q: A proton moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in a uniform magnetic field of strength 40 mT. The velocity of the proton makes an angle of 25° with the direction of the field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the proton? Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.why:
Students associate 'component along a direction' with cos θ from work and resolving forces, and use cos θ whenever an angle to a line is given. Only motion across the field produces a force: the force is zero for motion along the field. The relevant component is v sin θ (or L sin θ), with θ measured from the field direction.

Working: B = 40 mT = 0.040 T; θ = 25° (angle between v and B). F = qvB sin θ = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹)(0.040 T)(sin 25°) = (1.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ N)(0.423) = 8.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ N.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field as given by F = qvB sin θ, where B is the magnetic field strength

items.q: An electron moves towards the right of the page, in the plane of the page, through a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. What is the direction of the magnetic force on the electron at that instant?
items.correct: Towards the bottom of the page
items.misconception: Towards the top of the page
items.why: Direction rules are taught for conventional current (the motion of positive charge), and students apply them to an electron's velocity without reversing the result. F = qvB sin θ contains the charge q, so the sign of q sets the sense of the force. Find the force as if the particle were positive, then reverse it for a negative particle (or treat the electron's motion as a conventional current in the opposite direction).
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field as given by F = qvB sin θ, where B is the magnetic field strength
items.random_wrong: Towards the left of the page

items.q: A proton moves with a velocity parallel to the field lines of a uniform magnetic field. No other fields act. Which describes its subsequent motion?
items.correct: It carries on in a straight line at constant speed, as no magnetic force acts.
items.misconception: It moves in a circle around the field lines, as any moving charge in a magnetic field does.
items.why: Textbook examples almost always show the perpendicular case, so the circle becomes associated with 'a charge in a magnetic field' in general, and the sin θ factor is overlooked. The force is qvB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the field. For θ = 0° (motion along the field lines) the force is zero, so there is no deflection at all.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field as given by F = qvB sin θ, where B is the magnetic field strength
items.random_wrong: It slows down steadily and stops, because the magnetic field acts against its motion.

items.q: A straight wire 0.40 m long carries a current of 3.0 A. Only 0.25 m of the wire lies inside a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.080 T, and the wire makes an angle of 30° with the direction of the field. What is the magnitude of the force on the wire?
items.why:
The symbol L is read as 'the length of the wire' and substituted without asking which part of the wire the field acts on. The force acts only on current in the field. Use the length of conductor within the field region; the rest of the wire contributes nothing.

Working: L = length in the field = 0.25 m; θ = 30°. F = BIL sin θ = (0.080 T)(3.0 A)(0.25 m)(sin 30°) = 0.060 N × 0.50 = 0.030 N = 3.0 × 10⁻² N.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field as given by F = BIL sin θ

items.q: A straight wire lies in the plane of the page and carries a current towards the right of the page. A uniform magnetic field in the plane of the page is directed towards the top of the page. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
items.correct: Out of the plane of the page
items.misconception: Towards the top of the page
items.why: The electric force on a positive charge is along the field, and a compass needle or iron filing lines up along a magnetic field, so students expect the magnetic force to push along the field lines too. The magnetic force on a moving charge or a current is perpendicular to both the field and the velocity (or current). A charge moving along the field lines feels no magnetic force at all.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field as given by F = BIL sin θ
items.random_wrong: Towards the right of the page

items.q: Two long straight parallel wires in air are 4.0 cm apart and carry currents of 5.0 A and 8.0 A. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on a 1.5 m length of the wire carrying 8.0 A? Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ for air.
items.why:
The left-hand side of the equation is written as a ratio F/L, and students stop once they have evaluated the right-hand side. Evaluate the force per unit length first, then multiply by the length of wire considered: F = (μ₀I₁I₂/2πr) × L.

Working: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) = (4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)(5.0 A)(8.0 A)/(2π × 0.040 m) = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × 40)/0.040 N m⁻¹ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹. F = (F/L) × L = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹ × 1.5 m = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ N.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.

items.q: A long straight wire lies in the plane of the page and carries a current towards the top of the page. Point P is 3.0 cm to the right of the wire and point Q is 3.0 cm to the left of it, both in the plane of the page. What is the direction of the magnetic field due to the current at P and at Q?
items.correct: At P it is into the page; at Q it is out of the page
items.misconception: At P it is to the right; at Q it is to the left
items.why: Students transfer the radial electric field pattern of a charge or charged wire to the magnetic field of a current. Plotting-compass investigations show circular field lines around a current-carrying wire. At a point beside a wire in the plane of the page, the field is therefore into or out of the page, not along the line from the wire.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.random_wrong: At both P and Q it points towards the top of the page

items.q: Two long straight parallel copper wires are 5.0 cm apart in air. One carries a current of 2.0 A and the other a current of 6.0 A, in the same direction. Which statement about the magnetic forces between the wires is correct?
items.correct: Each wire is pulled towards the other by a force of the same magnitude.
items.misconception: The wires push each other apart, as their currents are in the same direction.
items.why: Students apply the rule 'like repels like', learned for charges and magnetic poles, to currents by analogy. Work it out rather than by analogy: find the field of one wire at the other, then the direction of F = BIL on the second wire. For currents in the same direction this force points towards the first wire, so the wires attract.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.random_wrong: Neither wire feels a force, as copper is not a magnetic material.

items.q: The diagram shows a proton moving through a region of uniform magnetic field B, which is represented by the dots. In which direction is the magnetic force on the proton at the instant shown?
items.correct: Towards the right of the page
items.misconception: Towards the left of the page
items.why: The convention is learned as a rule ("dots out, crosses in") without the picture of the arrow behind it, and a rule with no reason is easily remembered the wrong way round; a cross also looks like a mark on the page rather than the back of an arrow leaving it. Picture the field as arrows. Looking at an arrow flying towards you, you see its point: a dot, so dots mean out of the page. Looking at one flying away, you see its feathers: a cross, so crosses mean into the page.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field as given by F = qvB sin θ, where B is the magnetic field strength
items.random_wrong: Towards the bottom of the page

items.q: The diagram shows the path of a charged particle that enters a region of uniform magnetic field at O, moving to the right, and strikes a detector. The dots represent the field. No other forces act on the particle. Which statement about the particle is correct?
items.correct: It carries a negative charge.
items.misconception: It slows down along the arc.
items.why: Most everyday forces met on moving objects are resistive (friction, drag), and the language of fields 'resisting' motion is common in descriptions of magnetic braking. The magnetic force qvB sin θ is always perpendicular to the velocity. It has no component along the motion, so it does no work and the speed stays constant; it only changes the direction of motion.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field

items.q: The diagram shows an electron entering, at O, the region between two parallel plates in a vacuum. The potential difference between the plates is 150 V. The electron enters midway between the plates at speed v, parallel to them, and leaves at the far end of the plates having been deflected by the distance marked. Gravity is negligible. What is v? Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
items.why:
Students misremember the relationship by analogy with W = Fd, or rearrange ΔV = Ed incorrectly, and the product 'looks right' because both quantities increase the effect. The field strength is the potential difference per unit distance between the plates, E = V/d. Moving the plates apart at the same potential difference weakens the field. A quick unit check helps: V m⁻¹ is volts divided by metres.

Working: From the diagram: plate separation d = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m, plate length L = 6.0 cm = 0.060 m, deflection y = 4.0 mm = 0.0040 m. Field between the plates E = V/d = 150/0.020 = 7500 V m⁻¹. Acceleration towards the positive plate a = eE/m_e = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 7500)/(9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.32 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². The horizontal velocity is unchanged, so the time between the plates is t = L/v, and the deflection is y = ½at² = ½a(L/v)². Hence v = L√(a/2y) = 0.060 × √(1.32 × 10¹⁵/(2 × 0.0040)) = 0.060 × 4.06 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field
items.working: From the diagram: plate separation d = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m, plate length L = 6.0 cm = 0.060 m, deflection y = 4.0 mm = 0.0040 m. Field between the plates E = V/d = 150/0.020 = 7500 V m⁻¹. Acceleration towards the positive plate a = eE/m_e = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 7500)/(9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.32 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². The horizontal velocity is unchanged, so the time between the plates is t = L/v, and the deflection is y = ½at² = ½a(L/v)². Hence v = L√(a/2y) = 0.060 × √(1.32 × 10¹⁵/(2 × 0.0040)) = 0.060 × 4.06 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

items.q: A straight wire of length 25 cm carries a current I and lies at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of strength B. The graph shows how the magnetic force F on the wire varies with I. What is B?
items.correct: 240 mT
items.misconception: 120 mT
items.why:
Most worked examples are for motion perpendicular to the field, where sin 90° = 1, so students learn F = qvB and F = BIL without the sin θ factor. Use the full relations F = qvB sin θ and F = BIL sin θ. The simplified forms qvB and BIL apply only when θ = 90°.

Working: F = BIL sin θ, so a graph of F against I is a straight line through the origin with gradient BL sin θ. From the graph, gradient = 0.120 N/4.0 A = 0.030 N A⁻¹. With L = 0.25 m and θ = 30°: B = gradient/(L sin θ) = 0.030/(0.25 × 0.50) = 0.24 T = 240 mT.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field as given by F = BIL sin θ
items.working: F = BIL sin θ, so a graph of F against I is a straight line through the origin with gradient BL sin θ. From the graph, gradient = 0.120 N/4.0 A = 0.030 N A⁻¹. With L = 0.25 m and θ = 30°: B = gradient/(L sin θ) = 0.030/(0.25 × 0.50) = 0.24 T = 240 mT.

items.q: The diagram shows three long straight parallel wires P, Q and R lying in the same plane, equally spaced, each carrying a current of the same magnitude I in the direction shown. What is the direction of the resultant magnetic force on wire Q?
items.correct: To the left, towards P
items.misconception: Upwards, along the wire Q
items.why: Students picture the current as a stream that drags or pushes the wire along with it, and the idea that a force causes motion in its own direction reinforces this. The force on each moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity, so the force on the wire is perpendicular to the current, and also perpendicular to the field.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.

items.q: The diagram shows a velocity selector. Positive ions enter the region between two charged plates moving to the right at speed v, midway between the plates; the crosses represent a uniform magnetic field B. Ions with speed v₀ pass straight through undeflected. Gravity is negligible. Which describes the path of an ion whose speed is greater than v₀?
items.correct: It curves towards the positive plate at the top
items.misconception: It curves towards the negative plate below
items.why: Students read the larger radius in r = mv/(qB) as evidence of a weaker force, confusing the amount of bending with the size of the force. F = qvB: at twice the speed the magnetic force is twice as large. The path is less curved because the required centripetal force mv²/r grows faster (as v²) than the magnetic force does.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields

items.q: Does a charged particle entering a uniform electric field move off in a straight line in the direction of the force?
items.correct: No. The force changes the velocity gradually: the velocity component along the field grows steadily while the component across the field is unchanged, so the path curves.
items.misconception: A force makes a body move at a steady velocity in the direction of the force, so the particle heads off in a straight line at an angle.
items.why: This is the intuitive Aristotelian 'force implies motion' idea documented in mechanics research: everyday experience of pushing objects against friction suggests that a steady force produces a steady velocity. A resultant force produces an acceleration, a = F/m, not a velocity. Because the force acts continuously, the velocity component along the field keeps increasing and the direction of motion keeps turning towards the field direction, giving a curved (parabolic) path.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a uniform electric field perpendicular to a particle's initial velocity change the component of velocity across the field?
items.correct: No. There is no force component perpendicular to the field lines, so the velocity component in that direction stays constant.
items.misconception: As the particle is pulled sideways by the field, its original (forward) velocity component decreases.
items.why: Students treat the motion as a single quantity that is 'shared' between directions, the same error that leads them to think a projectile's horizontal velocity decreases during flight. Perpendicular components of motion are independent. The electric force acts only along the field lines, so it changes only the velocity component along the field; the component across the field is constant, which is why the time spent between the plates is length ÷ entry speed.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the magnetic force on a charged particle do work on it?
items.correct: No. The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the work done is zero and the kinetic energy is unchanged.
items.misconception: Because the magnetic force accelerates the particle, it must do work on it and increase its kinetic energy.
items.why: Students link 'force', 'acceleration' and 'speeding up' through everyday language, and learn W = Fs without the condition that the force must have a component along the displacement. Work done = Fs cos θ. The magnetic force is at 90° to the displacement at every instant, so cos 90° = 0 and no work is done. The acceleration is centripetal: it changes the direction of the velocity, not its magnitude.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field depend on its speed?
items.correct: Yes. r = mv/(qB), so the radius is proportional to the speed.
items.misconception: The radius of the circle is fixed by the magnetic field alone, so particles of every speed follow the same circle.
items.why: Diagrams of a single circular path in a field suggest that the circle belongs to the field, in the same way that a field line is drawn once for the field. The circle is set by the balance qvB = mv²/r. A faster particle needs a larger centripetal force mv²/r; the magnetic force grows only in proportion to v, so the circle must be larger: r = mv/(qB).
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a faster charged particle take less time to complete one circle in a uniform magnetic field?
items.correct: No. T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB): the radius increases in proportion to the speed, so the time for one revolution is independent of speed.
items.misconception: A faster particle must complete its circle in less time, because it is moving faster.
items.why: Everyday experience (a faster runner laps a fixed track sooner) is applied without noticing that in a magnetic field the track itself grows with the speed. Time = distance ÷ speed. The distance 2πr grows in proportion to v, so 2πr/v is unchanged: T = 2πm/(qB) depends only on the charge-to-mass ratio and the field.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the speed selected by crossed electric and magnetic fields depend on the charge or mass of the particle?
items.correct: No. A particle passes undeflected when qE = qvB, so v = E/B: the charge cancels and the mass does not appear. Particles of any charge (either sign) and any mass moving at E/B pass straight through.
items.misconception: A velocity selector passes only particles with a particular charge-to-mass ratio, so particles of a different mass or charge need a different speed.
items.why: The velocity selector is usually met as the first stage of a mass spectrometer, where the radius r = mv/(qB) in the magnetic field alone does depend on q/m, so students attach the q/m dependence to the selector as well. Write the balance condition: qE = qvB gives v = E/B, independent of q and m. The selector sorts by speed; sorting by charge-to-mass ratio happens afterwards, in the magnetic field alone.
items.specStatementText: the motion of a charged particle in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the direction of the current in a wire the direction in which the electrons move?
items.correct: No. The current direction is the conventional current, the direction in which positive charge would flow; in a metal the electrons drift the opposite way.
items.misconception: The current flows in the direction in which the electrons move.
items.why: Students learn that the charge carriers in metals are electrons and then equate 'current direction' with 'electron direction', especially after atomic-scale descriptions of conduction. The direction of I is conventional current. Treating the given current direction as the electron direction reverses the current and so reverses every force found from it.
items.specStatementText: the magnitude and direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field as given by F = BIL sin θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the force between two long parallel wires follow an inverse-square law?
items.correct: No. For long parallel wires the force per unit length is inversely proportional to the separation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr).
items.misconception: All field forces fall off with the square of the distance, so the force between wires is proportional to 1/r².
items.why: Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law, both inverse-square, are the first field laws students meet, and they generalise the 1/r² dependence to every field force. The inverse-square law applies to point masses and point charges. The field of a long straight wire falls as 1/r, so the force per unit length between parallel wires is proportional to 1/r.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the magnetic field produced by a current in a straight wire parallel to the current?
items.correct: No. The field lines circle the wire, so the field is perpendicular to the current at every point.
items.misconception: The magnetic field of a current points along the wire, in the direction of the current.
items.why: Students picture the field as 'carried along' with the current, and the arrow drawn on the wire for the current is the most visible arrow in the diagram. The field of a straight current forms circles in planes perpendicular to the wire; nowhere does it point along the wire.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the magnetic field of a straight wire in the same direction on both sides of the wire?
items.correct: No. The field lines are circles around the wire, so on opposite sides of a wire in the plane of the page the field points in opposite directions: into the page on one side and out on the other.
items.misconception: The field of the wire points the same way (for example, into the page) everywhere around it.
items.why: Converting a three-dimensional circular field into the 'into/out of the page' symbols of a two-dimensional diagram is difficult, and research on students' ideas about magnetic fields reports this trouble with spatial representation. Follow one circular field line around the wire: where it passes on one side it is heading into the page, and on the opposite side the same circle is heading out of the page.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When two parallel wires carry different currents, does the wire with the larger current exert the larger force?
items.correct: No. The forces on the two wires form a Newton's third law pair, so they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction; F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) is symmetric in I₁ and I₂.
items.misconception: The wire with the larger current, and therefore the stronger field, exerts a larger force on the other wire than it receives.
items.why: This is the familiar Newton's third law error documented in mechanics research (the 'stronger' or 'more active' body exerts more force), transferred to wires. The larger current produces the stronger field, but the smaller current sits in that field; the product I₁I₂ is the same for both wires. The forces are equal in magnitude, as Newton's third law requires.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can two copper wires exert magnetic forces on each other?
items.correct: Yes. A current produces a magnetic field and a current in a magnetic field experiences a force, whatever the material of the conductor.
items.misconception: Copper is not a magnetic material, so copper wires cannot exert magnetic forces on each other.
items.why: Early experience of magnets that attract only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt leads students to think magnetic forces act only on magnetic materials. Magnetic forces act on moving charges. The current in each copper wire produces a magnetic field, and the current in the other wire experiences a force F = BIL in that field.
items.specStatementText: the force per unit length between parallel wires as given by F/L = μ₀ I₁I₂/2πr where r is the separation between the two wires.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the force calculated from F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) shared between the two wires?
items.correct: No. It is the force on each wire. Each wire feels the full force, and the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (a Newton's third law pair).
items.misconception: The calculated force between two wires is shared between them, so each wire feels half of it.
items.why: The equation contains both currents and gives a single number for a two-wire system, so students read it as one interaction force to be divided between the wires, in the way a shared load is divided. The idea that the two forces of a Newton's third law pair are two halves of one force is a common misreading of the law. F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) is the force per unit length on either wire due to the field of the other. Each wire experiences this full force; the forces on the two wires are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, not two halves of one force.

items.q: Do two parallel current-carrying wires always attract each other?
items.correct: No. The force is attractive when the currents are in the same direction and repulsive when they are in opposite directions.
items.misconception: Parallel current-carrying wires always attract each other, whatever the directions of their currents.
items.why: The result "parallel currents attract" is remembered as a headline without its condition, and the familiar picture of two attracting wires used to introduce the ampere reinforces the idea that attraction is the only outcome. Find the field of one wire at the other with the right-hand grip rule, then apply F = BIL to the second wire. Reversing either current reverses the force, so currents in the same direction attract and currents in opposite directions repel.
